extracted.intended_audience: math olympiad students, trainers, and combinatorics problem-solvers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and principles (pigeonhole/box principle and enumerative combinatorics) for creating, selecting, and solving Olympiad-style combinatorics problems; includes concrete counting paradigms and common traps illustrated with examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: What is a good Olympiad problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Its solution should not require any prerequisites except cleverness. A high school student should not be at a disadvantage compared to a professional mathematician.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An ideal IMO problem should be unknown to all students; even a similar problem should never have been discussed in any country. The motive of a problem being well known is a reason not to use it. Scoring should reflect relative difficulty (examples: E1 suggested 6 points, hardest problem 8 points).

rubrics_metrics.name: Box Principle (Pigeonhole Principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: If objects are placed into fewer boxes than objects, some box contains at least two objects — used to force coincidences or bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply via many concrete devices illustrated in examples: subdivide intervals into equal parts and use fractional parts; consider residues modulo k; partition by last digits (endings) of numbers; project geometric objects onto a line and compare total projected lengths; count colored cells/rows to force repetitions; use area/measure arguments to bound how many objects can avoid overlap. Use parity, modular arithmetic, geometric projections, and clever box definitions tailored to the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide and Conquer (Super principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Split a problem into smaller parts, solve the parts, and combine the solutions for the whole problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This umbrella paradigm contains many specific combinatorial techniques such as sum rule, product rule, recursion, sieving, graph constructions. Trainers should teach its many instantiations and encourage recognizing opportunities to split problems into simpler subproblems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum Rule
rubrics_metrics.description: If A = A1 ∪ A2 ∪ ... ∪ Ar is a partition, then |A| = |A1| + |A2| + ... + |Ar|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to split a counting problem into disjoint cases (blocks/parts) so that each part is easier to count. The rule is ubiquitous and should be pointed out frequently in training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product Rule
rubrics_metrics.description: If a word or object has r positions and there are n_i independent choices for the i-th position, then the total number of objects is n1·n2·...·nr.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when choices for successive pieces are independent of prior choices. Use to count sequences, arrangements, and to build larger structures from independent components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recursion
rubrics_metrics.description: Split a problem into smaller copies of the same problem repeatedly until trivial, then combine to get the whole answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical in deriving recurrences; use for counting structures built inductively. Example: pairings count P_n satisfies P_n = (2n-1)P_{n-1}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting by Bijection
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is a bijection between two sets A and B and |B| is known, then |A| = |B|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct explicit bijections (combinatorial proofs) to transform a hard counting problem into a known count. Sometimes a p–q bijection (near-bijection) suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting the same objects in two different ways
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute the size of a set by two independent counting arguments to obtain identities or bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to derive combinatorial identities and inequalities; typical examples are double-counting arguments (e.g., counting edges of a bipartite relation both by rows and by columns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product–Sum Rule (Multiply along paths, add up path products)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret objects as directed paths in a graph: multiply along path choices (product) and sum over different path families (sum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model counting problems with layered graphs where each path corresponds to a combinatorial object; the total count is the sum of products of local choice counts along each path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ordering trap (account for symmetries by division)
rubrics_metrics.description: When you introduce an ordering to make counting easier, remember to eliminate multiple counting by dividing by the permutations you introduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by pairing example: ordering 2n players yields (2n)! arrangements but each pairing is counted 2^n n! times, so divide by that factor. Common trap in enumerative combinatorics—always check for implicit orderings and divide by symmetry factors.
